hero.title: Nigeria's opposition faces fresh court tests as global tensions intensify
hero.subtitle: The evening briefing examines three distinct ADC legal disputes, opposition coordination, security and accountability in Nigeria, and major developments across Europe, North America, Asia and the Middle East.
hero.description: A verified evening report on the Atiku eligibility case, the ADC leadership appeal and Adamawa nomination order, plus the Gombe and Bayelsa incidents, France's political contest, UK–EU relations, Ukraine, Gaza, Gulf shipping, AI markets and COP31.
hero.imageNote: No single verified photograph represents this multi-region edition; no unrelated image has been substituted.
hero.category: Nigeria / Africa / Europe / Americas / Asia / Middle East

morningSummary:
Good evening. Nigeria's opposition politics is again under legal scrutiny, but three separate court matters must not be confused. The Federal High Court refused Atiku Abubakar and the ADC permission to amend their challenge to President Bola Tinubu's 2027 eligibility; the substantive case remains pending and the judge did not rule on the authenticity of the NYSC certificate. In a separate Adamawa case, another judge ordered the ADC to restore Omar Suleiman as its governorship candidate. The national leadership dispute involving David Mark is before the Court of Appeal, with INEC saying it will await the appellate outcome while the rival faction demands immediate enforcement of the trial judgment.

The Coalition for Democracy has moved its second summit to 30 November and says participating parties—including the ADC, APM, NDC, a PDP faction, PRP and SDP—will pause campaign activity for the day. The meeting is expected to finalise a common agreement, but no common presidential candidate has been announced. Peter Obi has set campaign targets of 10,000 megawatts of electricity, 10,000 primary healthcare centres and 40,000 primary-school blocks; the public still needs costings and a delivery timetable. In Ibadan, President Tinubu made an unnamed 'palẹmọ' remark that some outlets interpreted as a swipe at Seyi Makinde's APM bid, although the President did not name him.

Nigeria also faces urgent public-safety and governance questions. Gombe State says three people died and 13 were injured in Lawanti after a confrontation involving residents and alleged military personnel; residents accuse Air Force personnel of opening fire, but the circumstances remain subject to official verification and the governor has ordered an impartial probe. In Bayelsa, police confirmed four deaths—including two children—and 24 rescues after a boat carrying mourners capsized. Customs has paused training for 3,852 recruits while it consults the Federal Character Commission over disputed exclusions and invitations.

In Africa, coalition negotiations in South Africa could keep the DA outside governing arrangements in Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni despite its position as the largest single party in each metro. Guinea has sentenced 224 people in an illegal gold-mining crackdown, while Ethiopia and Sudan continue to trade accusations about support for armed groups; the latter claims have not been independently verified and both governments deny wrongdoing.

In Europe, French prosecutors are investigating suspected leaks of confidential information to Marine Le Pen's National Rally, but no one had been formally charged in the reports reviewed. Separate protests over living costs and student rights drew lower turnout on Saturday, with official and organisers' estimates differing. The UK and EU have agreed a package on food trade, carbon markets and youth mobility; the youth scheme is for eligible UK and EU citizens aged 18–31 and is not due to begin before 2030. In Ukraine, local officials say a Russian strike on Kryvyi Rih killed two people and wounded 60.

In North America, President Donald Trump's new order requires federal contractors to coordinate with the White House before responding to certain congressional inquiries, raising a fresh test of executive privilege and legislative oversight. In Canada, Mark Carney's effort to diversify trade through closer engagement with China has prompted a warning from Taiwan that dependence can create political leverage; that warning is a policy assessment, not proof of coercion in Canada.

In Asia, Australia and China have agreed to establish a bilateral dialogue on AI safety, governance and applications while continuing to manage wider strategic differences. Japan and India have signed a letter of intent that would allow Japanese forces to conduct live-fire training at Indian ranges, including surface-to-ship missile exercises, once arrangements are implemented.

In the Middle East, Reuters reports that an Israeli strike hit a Gaza vehicle carrying food and killed three people according to the Gaza Health Ministry. Witnesses saw World Central Kitchen branding, but WCK said the vehicle was not affiliated with it; Israel said it was targeting Islamic Jihad, a claim Reuters could not independently verify. UKMTO has reported two tanker incidents near Oman's Khasab, but responsibility remains unknown. In Iraq, a fire at the Hartha power station killed four and injured 35, prompting an official investigation.

Business and technology markets remain volatile. The Nasdaq fell 5.3% on Friday and 10% for the week as investors reassessed AI valuations and spending, while oil benchmarks were on track for a third weekly decline on strong Middle East exports. COP31 negotiations in Antalya continued beyond the scheduled close, with countries divided over fossil-fuel language and climate-adaptation finance. As of this edition's 19:39 CET verification point, no final cover decision had been confirmed.

featured.title: Federal High Court rejects Atiku and ADC bid to amend Tinubu eligibility case
featured.summary: Justice Inyang Ekwo refused the proposed amendments to Atiku Abubakar and the ADC's pre-election suit, but did not decide whether the NYSC discharge certificate at the centre of the case is genuine.
featured.content:
Atiku Abubakar and the African Democratic Congress filed their suit against President Bola Tinubu, the All Progressives Congress and INEC on 14 August. They allege that the APC submitted a forged National Youth Service Corps discharge certificate in support of Tinubu's nomination, with the document bearing the name “Tinubu Bola Adekunle”. Tinubu and the APC deny submitting a forged certificate and say the NYSC has not denied issuing the discharge certificate.

On 20 November, Justice Inyang Ekwo rejected the plaintiffs' application to amend the case, ruling that the proposed changes would introduce fresh facts after the Constitution's 14-day limit for pre-election matters had expired. The judge directed the parties to proceed on the original filings. This is a procedural ruling: it is not a finding that the certificate is forged, and it is not a final judgment on Tinubu's eligibility.

featured.imageNote: RadiantWaves repository portrait; not a photograph of the court hearing.
featured.source: Premium Times, 20–21 November 2026; Tinubu and APC's denial reported in the court coverage
featured.whyItMatters: The distinction between a procedural ruling and a decision on the evidence is essential to fair reporting on presidential eligibility and the rule of law.
featured.whatHappensNext: The substantive suit remains before the Federal High Court. The next substantive hearing and any further applications will determine how the original evidence is tested.
featured.label: ADC / TINUBU ELIGIBILITY

topStories.title: Court orders ADC to restore Omar Suleiman as Adamawa governorship candidate
topStories.summary: The Federal High Court ordered INEC to recognise Omar Suleiman as the ADC's Adamawa candidate after finding no valid basis for replacing the primary winner with Tukur Ribadu.
topStories.content:
Justice Obiora Egwuatu ordered the ADC to forward Omar Suleiman's details to INEC and directed the commission not to recognise or publish Tukur Ribadu as the party's Adamawa governorship candidate. Suleiman had won the party primary in May, polling 143,216 votes across the state's 21 local government areas, according to the court report. Ribadu finished second with 56,801.

The judge found no evidence that Ribadu had successfully challenged the primary result through a properly constituted party appeal committee. The ADC and Ribadu argued that an appeal process had taken place, but affidavits from the primary committee's chairman and secretary said no such committee had been constituted. The order concerns the Adamawa governorship nomination; it is separate from the national ADC leadership appeal involving David Mark.
topStories.imageNote: No verified portrait of Omar Suleiman or photograph of the judgment is available in the repository.
topStories.whyItMatters: The ruling is a reminder that internal party primaries and nomination procedures are subject to legal scrutiny, including when party executives later change a result.
topStories.whatHappensNext: Watch for any appeal or further INEC action. The report reviewed for this edition records the Federal High Court order but does not establish whether an appeal has since been filed.
topStories.label: ADC / ADAMAWA NOMINATION

topStories.title: INEC awaits Court of Appeal as rival ADC factions dispute David Mark leadership
topStories.category: Nigeria / Politics / ADC / Electoral Commission / Judiciary
topStories.summary: INEC says it has been served notice of the appeal against the judgment that nullified David Mark's ADC leadership; the Nafiu Bala Gombe faction says the existing order should be enforced immediately.
topStories.content:
The Federal High Court judgment of 5 November nullified the Mark-led caretaker leadership and set aside actions taken under it. The Mark-led faction has filed an appeal and sought a stay of execution. INEC National Commissioner Mohammed Haruna told PUNCH that the commission had received notice of the appeal and would await the Court of Appeal's decision before determining its next step.

The rival faction led by Nafiu Bala Gombe argues that the judgment remains valid and binding because no superior court has stayed or set it aside. It wants INEC to recognise its leadership and remove Mark and former Interior Minister Rauf Aregbesola from the commission's records. The two sides therefore disagree both on the practical effect of the trial court's order and on what INEC should do while the appeal is pending. The appellate court has not yet delivered a final decision in the reports reviewed.
topStories.imageAlt: Repository image associated with Atiku Abubakar and David Mark
topStories.imageNote: Existing RadiantWaves image; illustrative of the party dispute, not a photograph of the appeal hearing.
topStories.whyItMatters: The dispute affects the authority to manage party records and nominations ahead of the 2027 election. It must be reported as an active legal contest, not as a settled political outcome.
topStories.whatHappensNext: The Court of Appeal must determine the appeal and any stay application. Until then, INEC's stated position is to await the appellate outcome, while the rival faction continues to demand immediate compliance with the trial judgment.
topStories.label: ADC / DAVID MARK APPEAL

topStories.title: Three reported dead and 13 injured after alleged shooting in Gombe community
topStories.summary: Residents allege that Nigerian Air Force personnel opened fire in Lawanti after a confrontation over suspected stolen armoured cables; Gombe's governor has ordered an impartial investigation.
topStories.content:
Preliminary information released by the Gombe State Government records three deaths and 13 injuries in Lawanti community, Akko Local Government Area. Residents told reporters that the incident followed a confrontation involving personnel of the Nigerian Air Force and people suspected of stealing armoured cables. Some residents allege that security personnel later returned and opened fire. Those allegations have not been independently established.

Governor Muhammadu Inuwa Yahaya condemned the loss of life, sent a delegation to the community and ordered a thorough, impartial and transparent investigation. The preliminary state report says the circumstances, causes of death and medical conditions of the injured remain subject to official verification. No public Nigerian Air Force response was located in the sources reviewed by 19:39 CET. The military's account and the findings of an independent inquiry are still needed.

topStories.source: Trust Radio / Daily Trust, 21 November 2026; Gombe State Government statement reported by The Sun and Daily Post
topStories.whyItMatters: The incident raises urgent questions about civilian protection, the use of force and accountability. The distinction between residents' allegations and facts established by an investigation is essential.
topStories.whatHappensNext: Publish the Nigerian Air Force's response when available, monitor the state inquiry and verify casualty details through medical and official records.

topStories.title: Bayelsa boat tragedy: four dead and 24 rescued as safety concerns intensify
topStories.category: Nigeria / Emergency / Transport / Bayelsa / Public Safety
topStories.summary: Police confirmed four deaths, including two children, and 24 rescues after a passenger boat capsized while carrying mourners to Ukubie in Southern Ijaw.
topStories.content:
The passenger boat was travelling from Ayama to Ukubie for a burial ceremony when it capsized near the Oweikorogha–Otuan river junction at about 11 a.m. on 20 November. Bayelsa police said four bodies—two adults and two children—had been recovered and 24 passengers rescued. Nineteen survivors were taken to Ayama Clinic and five injured people to Family Care Hospital in Yenagoa.

Police said preliminary information pointed to a mechanical fault, and the circumstances remain under investigation. The state government warned operators against overloading, reckless navigation and travelling without life jackets. Reports that the vessel may have been carrying far more passengers than its safe capacity require further confirmation; police have not published a verified passenger manifest.
topStories.imageNote: No verified scene photograph is available in the repository; do not use a generic river or boat image as if it showed this accident.
topStories.source: PUNCH, 20–21 November 2026; Bayelsa State Police Command; Al Jazeera, 20 November 2026
topStories.whyItMatters: Waterway safety depends on enforcement of passenger limits, seaworthy boats, life jackets and rapid rescue capacity. Repeated warnings are not a substitute for inspections.
topStories.whatHappensNext: Police should publish the outcome of the investigation, confirm the number of passengers and clarify whether the operator or boat manager faces charges.
topStories.label: BAYELSA / BOAT SAFETY

topStories.title: COP31 talks remain in overtime as fossil-fuel language and climate finance divide countries
topStories.summary: Nearly 200 countries remain divided over whether the final text should address fossil fuels and provide adaptation finance; no final cover decision had been agreed by the latest Reuters update.
topStories.content:
COP31 in Antalya continued beyond its scheduled Friday finish. Reuters reported on Saturday that negotiators were still divided over whether the final agreement should mention fossil fuels and include support for poorer countries adapting to climate change. A draft published on Thursday removed earlier references to ending fossil-fuel use and dropped a proposed $120 billion adaptation-finance target.

EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said the summit should produce a good deal or no deal. Türkiye's COP31 President Murat Kurum urged countries not to let disputes over wording derail the process. Gambia's finance negotiator warned that delay tactics could exhaust delegates into accepting a weaker text. As of the latest report reviewed for this 19:39 CET edition, a revised cover text had not been agreed. The UNFCCC lists the conference dates as 9–20 November, but negotiations continued into the weekend.
topStories.imageNote: No verified COP31 photograph has been added to the repository for this edition; a generic UN image would not document the negotiations.
topStories.whyItMatters: The outcome matters to countries facing floods, droughts and rising adaptation costs. Removing fossil-fuel language and weakening finance proposals would have consequences for climate ambition and trust between developed and developing states.
topStories.whatHappensNext: Watch for a revised cover decision, the response of vulnerable countries and whether a consensus text is adopted. Until a formal decision is published, no final COP31 deal should be claimed.
topStories.label: COP31 / NO FINAL DEAL CONFIRMED

topStories.title: Russian strike on Zelenskyy's hometown kills two and wounds 60, Ukrainian officials say
topStories.category: Europe / Ukraine / War / Security / Civilian Protection
topStories.summary: Local officials said a Russian strike on Kryvyi Rih killed a seven-year-old boy and a 20-year-old woman and wounded 60 people, including six children.
topStories.content:
A Russian strike hit central Kryvyi Rih, the hometown of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, local officials said on Saturday. Two people were killed and 60 wounded, including six children. The attack caused fires and damaged about 25 apartment buildings, a hospital, schools, businesses and vehicles, according to the regional and city authorities.

The Associated Press also reported that a Russian cargo ship bound for Kaliningrad caught fire in the Gulf of Finland after a drone attack, but responsibility for that incident was not established. Finland said the vessel drifted into its territorial waters and that rescue and environmental precautions were under way. These incidents add to regional security concerns as diplomatic efforts to end the war continue.

topStories.title: Israeli strike kills three Palestinians in Gaza vehicle carrying food, witnesses say
topStories.category: Middle East / Gaza / Conflict / Humanitarian Affairs
topStories.summary: Gaza's Health Ministry reported three deaths after an Israeli strike hit a truck carrying food; World Central Kitchen said the vehicle was not affiliated with the charity.
topStories.content:
Israeli forces struck a truck in Gaza City on 21 November. The Gaza Health Ministry said three people were killed. Witnesses told Reuters that the vehicle carried food and papers bearing the World Central Kitchen logo, but the charity said the truck was not affiliated with it. WCK said the driver had previously worked for the organisation and that the two other occupants were not its employees.

The Israeli military said it was targeting Islamic Jihad militants and that the vehicle had been transporting food to members of the group. Reuters said it could not independently verify the military's account, and Islamic Jihad did not immediately comment. The incident occurred despite the October 2025 US-backed ceasefire, which halted major fighting but has not ended Israeli attacks or resolved the question of Hamas disarmament.

topStories.source: Reuters, 21 November 2026; World Central Kitchen statement; Israeli military statement
topStories.whyItMatters: The competing accounts underline the need to verify the target, the vehicle's role and the identities of those killed. Aid branding alone does not prove that a vehicle was operated by a humanitarian organisation.
topStories.whatHappensNext: Watch for the Israeli military's further evidence, WCK's clarification and any independent investigation into the strike.

topStories.title: Trump order requires federal contractors to consult White House before answering Congress
topStories.category: United States / Politics / Governance / Congress / Accountability
topStories.summary: An executive order directs federal contractors to coordinate with the administration on congressional inquiries and withhold communications the White House considers privileged.
topStories.content:
President Donald Trump signed an executive order requiring federal contractors and subcontractors to consult the White House and relevant agencies before responding to certain congressional inquiries. The order says companies must coordinate appropriate responses and withhold communications the administration considers protected by executive privilege. It warns that contracts could be terminated and future federal work suspended for non-compliance.

The White House says the measure protects executive-branch confidentiality. The Associated Press reports that Democrats are preparing oversight investigations after taking control of Congress in January and have identified federal contracts as a major area of scrutiny. Executive privilege has been used by presidents of both parties, but its scope is not unlimited. The order is likely to be tested against Congress's constitutional oversight powers and may lead to legal disputes.

topStories.imageNote: RadiantWaves repository portrait; not a photograph of the executive-order signing.
topStories.whyItMatters: The order affects the information Congress can obtain from companies receiving public money and raises questions about the boundary between executive confidentiality and legislative oversight.
topStories.whatHappensNext: Watch for congressional responses, contract disputes and any court challenge. The order does not itself settle the constitutional limits of executive privilege.
topStories.label: USA / CONGRESSIONAL OVERSIGHT

topStories.title: UK and EU agree package on food trade, carbon markets and youth mobility
topStories.category: Europe / United Kingdom / European Union / Trade / Migration
topStories.summary: The UK government says the package could add up to £17 billion a year to the economy by 2040; its youth scheme is limited to eligible UK and EU citizens aged 18–31.
topStories.content:
At the UK–EU Summit in Brussels on 20 November, Prime Minister Andy Burnham and EU leaders concluded negotiations on a package covering food and agricultural trade, carbon-market links, youth experience and closer cooperation on migration and security. The UK government estimates that the package could add up to 0.5% of GDP by 2040, or around £17 billion a year; this is a projection, not guaranteed revenue.

The proposed Youth Experience Scheme would allow UK and EU citizens aged 18 to 31 when they first travel to live, work, study, volunteer or travel in each other's territories for up to three years. The scheme is expected to cover 100,000 participants from each side annually, with first travel expected no later than January 2030. It does not provide access to benefits or allow participants to bring dependants. The carbon-market link is being prepared for operation from 1 January 2028, subject to legislative and technical processes.

topStories.imageNote: RadiantWaves repository portrait; not a photograph of the UK–EU summit.
topStories.source: UK Prime Minister's Office / GOV.UK, 20 November 2026
topStories.whyItMatters: The agreement is a significant adjustment to post-Brexit relations, but its benefits depend on implementation, legal texts and the distribution of opportunities.
topStories.whatHappensNext: Watch for publication of the legal agreements, national approval processes and detailed application rules. Do not treat the youth scheme as available before the announced implementation timetable.

worldNews.title: UKMTO reports two tanker incidents near Oman's Khasab as Strait of Hormuz risk persists
worldNews.category: Middle East / Oman / Maritime Security / Energy
worldNews.summary: UKMTO reported two tanker incidents near Khasab involving unidentified projectiles; no casualties were reported and the environmental impact was not yet known.
worldNews.content:
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency reported that a tanker sailing out through the Strait of Hormuz was hit on its stern about 11 nautical miles north of Oman's Khasab. It later reported a second incident involving a tanker struck in its engine room about 17 nautical miles east of Khasab. It was not immediately clear whether the reports involved the same vessel.

UKMTO said no casualties had been reported and the environmental impact was unknown. Iran's navy separately said an oil tanker had caught fire after hitting a naval mine in a restricted area east of the strait, but Reuters could not independently verify the Iranian account or establish whether it referred to either UKMTO incident. No responsible party has been confirmed.
worldNews.imageAlt: Oil tanker image from the RadiantWaves Hormuz asset library
worldNews.imageNote: Existing repository tanker image; illustrative regional image, not a photograph of either reported incident.
worldNews.source: Reuters, 21 November 2026; UK Maritime Trade Operations
worldNews.whyItMatters: The Strait of Hormuz is a major energy shipping route. Unverified incident reports can move markets, but responsibility and the environmental consequences must be established before conclusions are drawn.
worldNews.whatHappensNext: Watch for UKMTO updates, vessel operator statements, environmental assessments and confirmation of whether the reports concern one or two ships.
worldNews.label: OMAN / HORMUZ SHIPPING

worldNews.title: Fire at Iraq's Hartha power station kills four and injures 35
worldNews.category: Middle East / Iraq / Energy / Infrastructure / Public Safety
worldNews.summary: Four people were killed and 35 injured after a fire at the Hartha power station north of Basra spread to nearby homes; Iraq's prime minister ordered an investigation.
worldNews.content:
Security officials told Reuters that the fire broke out at about 6 a.m. on 21 November at the Hartha power station north of Basra. It spread to neighbouring homes, and many casualties suffered burns or smoke inhalation. Civil defence teams brought the blaze under control, but operations at the station were halted.

Iraq's Electricity Ministry said the incident involved a gas pipeline supplying the facility. Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered an urgent investigation to establish the cause and responsibility. The station has an installed capacity of 800 megawatts and had been operating at about 400 megawatts before the fire. Officials had not yet published the full extent of the damage or a definitive cause.
worldNews.imageNote: No verified photograph of the Hartha fire is available in the repository; avoid using unrelated power-station imagery.
worldNews.source: Reuters, 21 November 2026; Iraq's Electricity Ministry and Security Media Cell, as reported by Reuters
worldNews.whyItMatters: The incident exposes the human and economic consequences of ageing energy infrastructure and the importance of maintenance, safety systems and transparent investigations.
worldNews.whatHappensNext: Watch for the investigation's findings, repairs to the gas pipeline and any effect on electricity supply in Basra and surrounding areas.
worldNews.label: IRAQ / POWER STATION FIRE

worldNews.title: France's cost-of-living and student-rights protests draw lower turnout
worldNews.category: Europe / France / Society / Politics / Public Services
worldNews.summary: Reuters reported 82,500 participants according to the Interior Ministry and 150,000 according to organisers at Saturday's largely peaceful demonstrations.
worldNews.content:
Demonstrations across France on 21 November focused on the cost of living and student rights. The Interior Ministry counted 82,500 participants nationwide, including 21,500 in Paris, while organisers estimated 150,000 across the country and 45,000 in the capital. Both figures were lower than the previous Saturday's reported turnout.

About 70,000 security personnel were deployed. Reuters described the marches as largely peaceful but reported sporadic violence, including in Marseille. The protests began in September with students demanding better school buildings, more teachers and university reforms, then broadened into a wider movement involving unions and activists concerned about living costs and police violence.

usaNews.title: Trump order requires federal contractors to consult White House before answering Congress
usaNews.category: United States / Politics / Governance / Congress / Accountability
usaNews.summary: An executive order directs federal contractors to coordinate with the administration on congressional inquiries and withhold communications the White House considers privileged.
usaNews.content:
President Donald Trump signed an executive order requiring federal contractors and subcontractors to consult the White House and relevant agencies before responding to certain congressional inquiries. The order says companies must coordinate appropriate responses and withhold communications the administration considers protected by executive privilege. It warns that contracts could be terminated and future federal work suspended for non-compliance.

The White House says the measure protects executive-branch confidentiality. The Associated Press reports that Democrats are preparing oversight investigations after taking control of Congress in January and have identified federal contracts as a major area of scrutiny. Executive privilege has been used by presidents of both parties, but its scope is not unlimited. The order is likely to be tested against Congress's constitutional oversight powers and may lead to legal disputes.

usaNews.whyItMatters: The order affects the information Congress can obtain from companies receiving public money and raises questions about the boundary between executive confidentiality and legislative oversight.
usaNews.whatHappensNext: Watch for congressional responses, contract disputes and any court challenge. The order does not itself settle the constitutional limits of executive privilege.

usaNews.title: AI-linked sell-off sends Nasdaq down 10% for the week, its steepest decline since 2020
usaNews.summary: Reuters reported a 5.3% Nasdaq fall on Friday and a 10% weekly decline, as investors reassessed AI valuations, data-centre spending and technology-sector risks.
usaNews.content:
Technology shares fell sharply on 20 November. Reuters reported that the Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.3% on Friday and 10% for the week, its steepest weekly decline since 2020. Nvidia fell 14% on the day and 23% for the week, while the semiconductor index lost 11%. Anthropic shares also declined after a high-profile market debut.

Investors cited concerns about high valuations, the pace of data-centre investment, the outlook for earnings and uncertainty surrounding Nvidia after reports of an SEC accounting probe. Some market professionals described the move as a repricing or technical correction rather than the end of the AI investment cycle. That is an interpretation, not a guarantee of recovery. The episode shows how concentrated market expectations around AI can amplify volatility across the wider market.

usaNews.title: US tightens rules on remote access to advanced AI chips through overseas data centres
usaNews.category: Technology / Artificial Intelligence / United States / China / Export Controls
usaNews.summary: New US rules require stronger controls on overseas data-centre access to advanced AI chips, as Washington seeks to limit diversion while Beijing criticises the measures.
usaNews.content:
Associated Press reported that the United States has tightened controls on remote access to advanced AI chips through overseas data centres and expanded licensing requirements affecting sales to several third countries. The rules are intended to prevent restricted computing capacity from being accessed indirectly by entities that cannot buy the chips directly.

China has criticised the measures as economic coercion. The regulatory dispute is part of a wider contest over advanced semiconductors, data-centre infrastructure and the governance of artificial intelligence. The existence of tighter rules does not establish that any named company has violated them; allegations of diversion require evidence and due process.

electionWatch.title: Federal High Court rejects Atiku and ADC bid to amend Tinubu eligibility case
electionWatch.summary: Justice Inyang Ekwo refused the proposed amendments to Atiku Abubakar and the ADC's pre-election suit, but did not decide whether the NYSC discharge certificate at the centre of the case is genuine.
electionWatch.content:
Atiku Abubakar and the African Democratic Congress filed their suit against President Bola Tinubu, the All Progressives Congress and INEC on 14 August. They allege that the APC submitted a forged National Youth Service Corps discharge certificate in support of Tinubu's nomination, with the document bearing the name “Tinubu Bola Adekunle”. Tinubu and the APC deny submitting a forged certificate and say the NYSC has not denied issuing the discharge certificate.

On 20 November, Justice Inyang Ekwo rejected the plaintiffs' application to amend the case, ruling that the proposed changes would introduce fresh facts after the Constitution's 14-day limit for pre-election matters had expired. The judge directed the parties to proceed on the original filings. This is a procedural ruling: it is not a finding that the certificate is forged, and it is not a final judgment on Tinubu's eligibility.
electionWatch.imageAlt: File portrait of former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar
electionWatch.imageNote: RadiantWaves repository portrait; not a photograph of the court hearing.
electionWatch.source: Premium Times, 20–21 November 2026; Tinubu and APC's denial reported in the court coverage
electionWatch.whyItMatters: The distinction between a procedural ruling and a decision on the evidence is essential to fair reporting on presidential eligibility and the rule of law.
electionWatch.whatHappensNext: The substantive suit remains before the Federal High Court. The next substantive hearing and any further applications will determine how the original evidence is tested.
electionWatch.label: ADC / TINUBU ELIGIBILITY

electionWatch.title: Court orders ADC to restore Omar Suleiman as Adamawa governorship candidate
electionWatch.summary: The Federal High Court ordered INEC to recognise Omar Suleiman as the ADC's Adamawa candidate after finding no valid basis for replacing the primary winner with Tukur Ribadu.
electionWatch.content:
Justice Obiora Egwuatu ordered the ADC to forward Omar Suleiman's details to INEC and directed the commission not to recognise or publish Tukur Ribadu as the party's Adamawa governorship candidate. Suleiman had won the party primary in May, polling 143,216 votes across the state's 21 local government areas, according to the court report. Ribadu finished second with 56,801.

The judge found no evidence that Ribadu had successfully challenged the primary result through a properly constituted party appeal committee. The ADC and Ribadu argued that an appeal process had taken place, but affidavits from the primary committee's chairman and secretary said no such committee had been constituted. The order concerns the Adamawa governorship nomination; it is separate from the national ADC leadership appeal involving David Mark.
electionWatch.imageNote: No verified portrait of Omar Suleiman or photograph of the judgment is available in the repository.
electionWatch.whyItMatters: The ruling is a reminder that internal party primaries and nomination procedures are subject to legal scrutiny, including when party executives later change a result.
electionWatch.whatHappensNext: Watch for any appeal or further INEC action. The report reviewed for this edition records the Federal High Court order but does not establish whether an appeal has since been filed.
electionWatch.label: ADC / ADAMAWA NOMINATION

electionWatch.title: INEC awaits Court of Appeal as rival ADC factions dispute David Mark leadership
electionWatch.category: Nigeria / Politics / ADC / Electoral Commission / Judiciary
electionWatch.summary: INEC says it has been served notice of the appeal against the judgment that nullified David Mark's ADC leadership; the Nafiu Bala Gombe faction says the existing order should be enforced immediately.
electionWatch.content:
The Federal High Court judgment of 5 November nullified the Mark-led caretaker leadership and set aside actions taken under it. The Mark-led faction has filed an appeal and sought a stay of execution. INEC National Commissioner Mohammed Haruna told PUNCH that the commission had received notice of the appeal and would await the Court of Appeal's decision before determining its next step.

The rival faction led by Nafiu Bala Gombe argues that the judgment remains valid and binding because no superior court has stayed or set it aside. It wants INEC to recognise its leadership and remove Mark and former Interior Minister Rauf Aregbesola from the commission's records. The two sides therefore disagree both on the practical effect of the trial court's order and on what INEC should do while the appeal is pending. The appellate court has not yet delivered a final decision in the reports reviewed.
electionWatch.imageAlt: Repository image associated with Atiku Abubakar and David Mark
electionWatch.imageNote: Existing RadiantWaves image; illustrative of the party dispute, not a photograph of the appeal hearing.
electionWatch.whyItMatters: The dispute affects the authority to manage party records and nominations ahead of the 2027 election. It must be reported as an active legal contest, not as a settled political outcome.
electionWatch.whatHappensNext: The Court of Appeal must determine the appeal and any stay application. Until then, INEC's stated position is to await the appellate outcome, while the rival faction continues to demand immediate compliance with the trial judgment.
electionWatch.label: ADC / DAVID MARK APPEAL

electionWatch.title: Opposition coalition moves Abuja summit to 30 November
electionWatch.category: Nigeria / Politics / Opposition / ADC / APM / NDC / PDP / Elections
electionWatch.summary: The Coalition for Democracy has postponed its second summit from 23 to 30 November and says member parties will pause campaign activities nationwide for the day.
electionWatch.content:
The Coalition for Democracy moved its second summit after member parties said campaign schedules could prevent presidential candidates, national chairmen and party leaders from attending. The committee's statement, signed by Salihu Moh. Lukman, says the gathering is intended to finalise and sign a common agreement ahead of the 16 January 2027 presidential election.

The coalition includes the ADC, Allied Peoples Movement, Nigeria Democratic Congress, a faction of the PDP, Peoples Redemption Party and Social Democratic Party. Organisers say participating parties have agreed to suspend campaigns nationwide on 30 November so leaders can attend. The announcement is evidence of coordination, but it is not yet proof that the parties have agreed on one presidential candidate or resolved their internal differences.
electionWatch.imageAlt: File portrait of Atiku Abubakar from the RadiantWaves image library
electionWatch.imageNote: One of the repository's separate Atiku photographs; used as an opposition-politics illustration, not a photograph of the summit.
electionWatch.whyItMatters: Opposition cooperation could widen voter choice, but its credibility will depend on transparent decision-making, a clear programme and respect for each party's internal democratic processes.
electionWatch.whatHappensNext: The key test is whether the 30 November meeting produces a signed agreement, an accountable structure and a clear process for resolving candidate and policy differences.
electionWatch.label: OPPOSITION COALITION

electionWatch.title: Peter Obi sets 10,000MW electricity target and makes health and education pledges
electionWatch.summary: At an Onitsha town hall, Peter Obi pledged 10,000 megawatts of electricity, 10,000 primary healthcare centres and 40,000 primary-school blocks if elected.
electionWatch.content:
Peter Obi, presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, outlined the targets during a homecoming and town-hall engagement in Onitsha. He said his administration would aim to generate, transmit and distribute at least 10,000 megawatts of electricity, build 10,000 primary healthcare centres and provide 40,000 primary-school blocks.

These are campaign commitments, not funded projects or completed government programmes. The published report did not provide a full costed plan, a construction timetable, a staffing model for the proposed health centres or a detailed financing strategy. Obi also urged supporters to remain at polling units until votes are counted and results transmitted. Voters should be able to compare these promises with budgets, delivery milestones and the candidate's record in public office.
electionWatch.imageNote: RadiantWaves repository portrait; not a photograph of the Onitsha town hall.
electionWatch.whyItMatters: Large infrastructure pledges are meaningful only when voters can see the costs, delivery timetable, staffing needs and measurable outcomes.
electionWatch.whatHappensNext: The NDC should publish costings, funding assumptions, timelines and state-by-state implementation targets so the public can test the proposal.
electionWatch.label: NDC / PETER OBI POLICY

electionWatch.title: Tinubu's Ibadan rally remark draws attention to Seyi Makinde's APM presidential bid
electionWatch.summary: President Tinubu referred to a 'palẹmọ' group at the Ibadan rally without naming Seyi Makinde or the APM; PUNCH and other outlets interpreted the remark as a swipe at the governor's presidential bid.
electionWatch.content:
President Bola Tinubu addressed an APC campaign rally at Mapo Hall in Ibadan on Saturday and urged Oyo voters to support the ruling party. He referred to an unnamed group or faction as the 'palẹmọ' group and said its members were waiting in vain. The President did not name Governor Seyi Makinde or the Allied Peoples Movement in the quoted remark.

Makinde is seeking the presidency under the APM platform. The political context makes the interpretation understandable, but a newsroom should distinguish the words actually spoken from the identity attributed to the target by commentators or reporters. The exchange is part of a competitive campaign; it does not alter the legal status of any candidate or party.
electionWatch.imageAlt: File portrait of Oyo State Governor Seyi Makinde
electionWatch.imageNote: RadiantWaves repository portrait; not a photograph of the Ibadan rally.
electionWatch.whyItMatters: The language of a campaign matters, but accuracy requires not attributing an unnamed remark to a person unless the speaker identifies them or the evidence establishes the target.
electionWatch.whatHappensNext: Watch for a direct response from Makinde or the APM and for any further campaign statements that clarify the exchange.
electionWatch.label: APM / MAKINDE CAMPAIGN

breakingHistory.summary: The three leaders met for their first trilateral summit and agreed to open dialogue on reducing nuclear risks. The meeting produced no announced breakthrough on Ukraine.
breakingHistory.content: US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin met in Shenzhen on 19 November during the APEC summit. Reporting from the meeting says the leaders agreed to open a dialogue on reducing the risks of nuclear weapons. The meeting was historic, but it did not produce a ceasefire or a breakthrough on Russia's war in Ukraine. The summit's declaration also addressed UN reform and energy cooperation. Ukraine and European security remain central issues in separate diplomatic discussions. The report should not be described as a peace agreement for Ukraine.

todaysBigQuestion: How can Nigeria's opposition build a credible alternative while protecting internal democracy, due process and peaceful competition?
thoughtForToday: Democracy is strongest when power is questioned with evidence, decisions are tested by law and citizens remain free to choose.
radiantWavesPerspective: RadiantWaves reports for the public, not for a political faction. Allegations must be attributed, responses included, court orders described accurately and legal status updated only when confirmed. Opposition parties deserve fair scrutiny and the same accountability expected of the government. A credible democracy requires lawful competition, independent institutions, transparent elections and peaceful participation.

articles.title: Federal High Court rejects Atiku and ADC bid to amend Tinubu eligibility case
articles.category: Nigeria / Politics / Elections / Judiciary
articles.summary: Justice Inyang Ekwo refused the proposed amendments to Atiku Abubakar and the ADC's pre-election suit, but did not decide whether the NYSC discharge certificate at the centre of the case is genuine.
articles.content:
Atiku Abubakar and the African Democratic Congress filed their suit against President Bola Tinubu, the All Progressives Congress and INEC on 14 August. They allege that the APC submitted a forged National Youth Service Corps discharge certificate in support of Tinubu's nomination, with the document bearing the name “Tinubu Bola Adekunle”. Tinubu and the APC deny submitting a forged certificate and say the NYSC has not denied issuing the discharge certificate.

On 20 November, Justice Inyang Ekwo rejected the plaintiffs' application to amend the case, ruling that the proposed changes would introduce fresh facts after the Constitution's 14-day limit for pre-election matters had expired. The judge directed the parties to proceed on the original filings. This is a procedural ruling: it is not a finding that the certificate is forged, and it is not a final judgment on Tinubu's eligibility.
articles.imageAlt: File portrait of former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar
articles.imageNote: RadiantWaves repository portrait; not a photograph of the court hearing.
articles.source: Premium Times, 20–21 November 2026; Tinubu and APC's denial reported in the court coverage
articles.whyItMatters: The distinction between a procedural ruling and a decision on the evidence is essential to fair reporting on presidential eligibility and the rule of law.
articles.whatHappensNext: The substantive suit remains before the Federal High Court. The next substantive hearing and any further applications will determine how the original evidence is tested.
articles.label: ADC / TINUBU ELIGIBILITY

articles.title: Court orders ADC to restore Omar Suleiman as Adamawa governorship candidate
articles.category: Nigeria / Politics / ADC / Elections / Judiciary
articles.summary: The Federal High Court ordered INEC to recognise Omar Suleiman as the ADC's Adamawa candidate after finding no valid basis for replacing the primary winner with Tukur Ribadu.
articles.content:
Justice Obiora Egwuatu ordered the ADC to forward Omar Suleiman's details to INEC and directed the commission not to recognise or publish Tukur Ribadu as the party's Adamawa governorship candidate. Suleiman had won the party primary in May, polling 143,216 votes across the state's 21 local government areas, according to the court report. Ribadu finished second with 56,801.

The judge found no evidence that Ribadu had successfully challenged the primary result through a properly constituted party appeal committee. The ADC and Ribadu argued that an appeal process had taken place, but affidavits from the primary committee's chairman and secretary said no such committee had been constituted. The order concerns the Adamawa governorship nomination; it is separate from the national ADC leadership appeal involving David Mark.
articles.imageNote: No verified portrait of Omar Suleiman or photograph of the judgment is available in the repository.
articles.whyItMatters: The ruling is a reminder that internal party primaries and nomination procedures are subject to legal scrutiny, including when party executives later change a result.
articles.whatHappensNext: Watch for any appeal or further INEC action. The report reviewed for this edition records the Federal High Court order but does not establish whether an appeal has since been filed.
articles.label: ADC / ADAMAWA NOMINATION

articles.title: INEC awaits Court of Appeal as rival ADC factions dispute David Mark leadership
articles.category: Nigeria / Politics / ADC / Electoral Commission / Judiciary
articles.summary: INEC says it has been served notice of the appeal against the judgment that nullified David Mark's ADC leadership; the Nafiu Bala Gombe faction says the existing order should be enforced immediately.
articles.content:
The Federal High Court judgment of 5 November nullified the Mark-led caretaker leadership and set aside actions taken under it. The Mark-led faction has filed an appeal and sought a stay of execution. INEC National Commissioner Mohammed Haruna told PUNCH that the commission had received notice of the appeal and would await the Court of Appeal's decision before determining its next step.

The rival faction led by Nafiu Bala Gombe argues that the judgment remains valid and binding because no superior court has stayed or set it aside. It wants INEC to recognise its leadership and remove Mark and former Interior Minister Rauf Aregbesola from the commission's records. The two sides therefore disagree both on the practical effect of the trial court's order and on what INEC should do while the appeal is pending. The appellate court has not yet delivered a final decision in the reports reviewed.
articles.imageAlt: Repository image associated with Atiku Abubakar and David Mark
articles.imageNote: Existing RadiantWaves image; illustrative of the party dispute, not a photograph of the appeal hearing.
articles.whyItMatters: The dispute affects the authority to manage party records and nominations ahead of the 2027 election. It must be reported as an active legal contest, not as a settled political outcome.
articles.whatHappensNext: The Court of Appeal must determine the appeal and any stay application. Until then, INEC's stated position is to await the appellate outcome, while the rival faction continues to demand immediate compliance with the trial judgment.
articles.label: ADC / DAVID MARK APPEAL

articles.title: Opposition coalition moves Abuja summit to 30 November
articles.category: Nigeria / Politics / Opposition / ADC / APM / NDC / PDP / Elections
articles.summary: The Coalition for Democracy has postponed its second summit from 23 to 30 November and says member parties will pause campaign activities nationwide for the day.
articles.content:
The Coalition for Democracy moved its second summit after member parties said campaign schedules could prevent presidential candidates, national chairmen and party leaders from attending. The committee's statement, signed by Salihu Moh. Lukman, says the gathering is intended to finalise and sign a common agreement ahead of the 16 January 2027 presidential election.

The coalition includes the ADC, Allied Peoples Movement, Nigeria Democratic Congress, a faction of the PDP, Peoples Redemption Party and Social Democratic Party. Organisers say participating parties have agreed to suspend campaigns nationwide on 30 November so leaders can attend. The announcement is evidence of coordination, but it is not yet proof that the parties have agreed on one presidential candidate or resolved their internal differences.
articles.imageAlt: File portrait of Atiku Abubakar from the RadiantWaves image library
articles.imageNote: One of the repository's separate Atiku photographs; used as an opposition-politics illustration, not a photograph of the summit.
articles.whyItMatters: Opposition cooperation could widen voter choice, but its credibility will depend on transparent decision-making, a clear programme and respect for each party's internal democratic processes.
articles.whatHappensNext: The key test is whether the 30 November meeting produces a signed agreement, an accountable structure and a clear process for resolving candidate and policy differences.
articles.label: OPPOSITION COALITION

articles.title: Peter Obi sets 10,000MW electricity target and makes health and education pledges
articles.category: Nigeria / Politics / NDC / Policy / Elections
articles.summary: At an Onitsha town hall, Peter Obi pledged 10,000 megawatts of electricity, 10,000 primary healthcare centres and 40,000 primary-school blocks if elected.
articles.content:
Peter Obi, presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, outlined the targets during a homecoming and town-hall engagement in Onitsha. He said his administration would aim to generate, transmit and distribute at least 10,000 megawatts of electricity, build 10,000 primary healthcare centres and provide 40,000 primary-school blocks.

These are campaign commitments, not funded projects or completed government programmes. The published report did not provide a full costed plan, a construction timetable, a staffing model for the proposed health centres or a detailed financing strategy. Obi also urged supporters to remain at polling units until votes are counted and results transmitted. Voters should be able to compare these promises with budgets, delivery milestones and the candidate's record in public office.
articles.imageNote: RadiantWaves repository portrait; not a photograph of the Onitsha town hall.
articles.whyItMatters: Large infrastructure pledges are meaningful only when voters can see the costs, delivery timetable, staffing needs and measurable outcomes.
articles.whatHappensNext: The NDC should publish costings, funding assumptions, timelines and state-by-state implementation targets so the public can test the proposal.
articles.label: NDC / PETER OBI POLICY

articles.title: Tinubu's Ibadan rally remark draws attention to Seyi Makinde's APM presidential bid
articles.category: Nigeria / Politics / APM / Elections / Opposition
articles.summary: President Tinubu referred to a 'palẹmọ' group at the Ibadan rally without naming Seyi Makinde or the APM; PUNCH and other outlets interpreted the remark as a swipe at the governor's presidential bid.
articles.content:
President Bola Tinubu addressed an APC campaign rally at Mapo Hall in Ibadan on Saturday and urged Oyo voters to support the ruling party. He referred to an unnamed group or faction as the 'palẹmọ' group and said its members were waiting in vain. The President did not name Governor Seyi Makinde or the Allied Peoples Movement in the quoted remark.

Makinde is seeking the presidency under the APM platform. The political context makes the interpretation understandable, but a newsroom should distinguish the words actually spoken from the identity attributed to the target by commentators or reporters. The exchange is part of a competitive campaign; it does not alter the legal status of any candidate or party.
articles.imageAlt: File portrait of Oyo State Governor Seyi Makinde
articles.imageNote: RadiantWaves repository portrait; not a photograph of the Ibadan rally.
articles.whyItMatters: The language of a campaign matters, but accuracy requires not attributing an unnamed remark to a person unless the speaker identifies them or the evidence establishes the target.
articles.whatHappensNext: Watch for a direct response from Makinde or the APM and for any further campaign statements that clarify the exchange.
articles.label: APM / MAKINDE CAMPAIGN

articles.title: Three reported dead and 13 injured after alleged shooting in Gombe community
articles.category: Nigeria / Security / Human Rights / Gombe
articles.summary: Residents allege that Nigerian Air Force personnel opened fire in Lawanti after a confrontation over suspected stolen armoured cables; Gombe's governor has ordered an impartial investigation.
articles.content:
Preliminary information released by the Gombe State Government records three deaths and 13 injuries in Lawanti community, Akko Local Government Area. Residents told reporters that the incident followed a confrontation involving personnel of the Nigerian Air Force and people suspected of stealing armoured cables. Some residents allege that security personnel later returned and opened fire. Those allegations have not been independently established.

Governor Muhammadu Inuwa Yahaya condemned the loss of life, sent a delegation to the community and ordered a thorough, impartial and transparent investigation. The preliminary state report says the circumstances, causes of death and medical conditions of the injured remain subject to official verification. No public Nigerian Air Force response was located in the sources reviewed by 19:39 CET. The military's account and the findings of an independent inquiry are still needed.
articles.imageNote: No verified photograph of the Lawanti incident is available; avoid using unrelated military or village images.
articles.source: Trust Radio / Daily Trust, 21 November 2026; Gombe State Government statement reported by The Sun and Daily Post
articles.whyItMatters: The incident raises urgent questions about civilian protection, the use of force and accountability. The distinction between residents' allegations and facts established by an investigation is essential.
articles.whatHappensNext: Publish the Nigerian Air Force's response when available, monitor the state inquiry and verify casualty details through medical and official records.
articles.label: GOMBE / ALLEGED SECURITY SHOOTING

articles.title: Bayelsa boat tragedy: four dead and 24 rescued as safety concerns intensify
articles.category: Nigeria / Emergency / Transport / Bayelsa / Public Safety
articles.summary: Police confirmed four deaths, including two children, and 24 rescues after a passenger boat capsized while carrying mourners to Ukubie in Southern Ijaw.
articles.content:
The passenger boat was travelling from Ayama to Ukubie for a burial ceremony when it capsized near the Oweikorogha–Otuan river junction at about 11 a.m. on 20 November. Bayelsa police said four bodies—two adults and two children—had been recovered and 24 passengers rescued. Nineteen survivors were taken to Ayama Clinic and five injured people to Family Care Hospital in Yenagoa.

Police said preliminary information pointed to a mechanical fault, and the circumstances remain under investigation. The state government warned operators against overloading, reckless navigation and travelling without life jackets. Reports that the vessel may have been carrying far more passengers than its safe capacity require further confirmation; police have not published a verified passenger manifest.
articles.imageNote: No verified scene photograph is available in the repository; do not use a generic river or boat image as if it showed this accident.
articles.source: PUNCH, 20–21 November 2026; Bayelsa State Police Command; Al Jazeera, 20 November 2026
articles.whyItMatters: Waterway safety depends on enforcement of passenger limits, seaworthy boats, life jackets and rapid rescue capacity. Repeated warnings are not a substitute for inspections.
articles.whatHappensNext: Police should publish the outcome of the investigation, confirm the number of passengers and clarify whether the operator or boat manager faces charges.
articles.label: BAYELSA / BOAT SAFETY

articles.title: Customs pauses training for 3,852 recruits amid Federal Character Commission dispute
articles.category: Nigeria / Governance / Public Service / Recruitment / Economy
articles.summary: The Nigeria Customs Service has temporarily halted training at two colleges after the Federal Character Commission raised concerns about who was invited from the 2024–2025 recruitment exercise.
articles.content:
The Nigeria Customs Service said it had temporarily put training activities at its two colleges on hold to allow further consultations with the Federal Character Commission. The exercise attracted 573,680 applications and produced 3,852 successful candidates across three cadres. The final lists were published in July 2026 and training began on 9 October.

The FCC says more than 500 applicants who completed screening and appeared on published lists were excluded from training, while some people whose names were not on the final lists allegedly received invitations. Customs has said a shortlist did not guarantee enlistment and that 397 applicants were screened out on eligibility grounds including age, medical status, physical fitness and documents. The FCC wants access to recruitment records and an independent audit. The Customs statement did not give a date for resuming training.
articles.imageNote: No verified image of the disputed recruitment process is available; an unrelated Customs photograph would not explain the allegations.
articles.source: PUNCH, 21 November 2026; Nairametrics, 20 November 2026; Federal Character Commission
articles.whyItMatters: The dispute tests the balance between merit, federal character, transparency and fair treatment of applicants who relied on published recruitment lists.

articles.title: ANC-led coalition talks threaten to shut the DA out of Gauteng's three metros
articles.category: Africa / South Africa / Politics / Local Government / Opposition
articles.summary: The ANC, ActionSA, EFF and MK Party have the numbers for majorities in Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni, while the DA warns that excluding it would disregard its status as the largest party in each metro.
articles.content:
Coalition negotiations in Gauteng have moved towards an arrangement involving the ANC, ActionSA, EFF, MK Party and other parties, potentially leaving the Democratic Alliance outside the governing coalitions in Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni. Mail & Guardian reported that the four main parties together hold 138 of 270 seats in Johannesburg, 128 of 224 in Ekurhuleni and 109 of 214 in Tshwane—enough for a majority in each council.

The DA won the largest single-party share in all three metros but did not secure an outright majority. DA leader Geordin Hill-Lewis says excluding the party would be a serious political error and voters will hold parties accountable. ActionSA leader Herman Mashaba says his party's coalition choices are driven by service delivery and its opposition to working with the DA while Helen Zille and Cilliers Brink remain central to its political calculations. The final distribution of mayoralties and portfolios remains subject to negotiations.

articles.whyItMatters: The negotiations show how proportional representation can produce coalitions that exclude the largest single party. Accountability will depend on whether the new councils deliver stable services and explain their power-sharing choices.

articles.title: Guinea sentences 224 people in crackdown on illegal gold mining
articles.category: Africa / Guinea / Environment / Mining / Courts
articles.summary: A court in Guinea handed prison terms to 202 miners and 22 former local officials in a case involving illegal gold mining, pollution and environmental damage.
articles.content:
Associated Press reported that 224 people were sentenced in Siguiri, a major gold-producing area in north-eastern Guinea. Twenty-two former local officials received two-year prison terms and fines for complicity in environmental degradation and water pollution. The 202 miners, including foreign nationals, received three-year sentences for illegal mining and related offences, with additional fines and, for foreign defendants, a 10-year ban from Guinea.

The crackdown follows arrests and clashes in which 10 people were reported killed and 13 injured. Illegal mining supports a large number of livelihoods, so enforcement carries social and economic consequences as well as environmental ones. The court sentences are established; claims about the wider scale of pollution and the impact on displaced miners should continue to be attributed to the relevant authorities and researchers.

articles.title: Ethiopia and Sudan trade unverified accusations over support for armed groups
articles.category: Africa / Horn of Africa / Security / Diplomacy
articles.summary: Sudan and Ethiopia accuse each other of aiding armed opponents, but the claims have not been independently verified and both governments deny wrongdoing.
articles.content:
Sudan says Ethiopia is hosting camps and enabling the Rapid Support Forces to launch drone and cross-border attacks. Ethiopia, in turn, accuses Sudan of supporting Tigrayan rebels after fighting resumed in September. Both governments deny the allegations, which Associated Press said it could not independently verify.

Sudan has taken its accusations to the United Nations and African Union, while Ethiopia has expelled Sudanese consular staff and closed the mission. The dispute is unfolding alongside Sudan's devastating war and renewed tension in Tigray. Analysts warn that weapons and fighters crossing borders could turn domestic conflicts into a wider proxy confrontation, but that remains a risk assessment rather than an established outcome.

articles.label: HORN OF AFRICA / SECURITY

articles.category: Europe / France / Politics / Judiciary / Opposition
articles.summary: Prosecutors are examining whether a former senior Interior Ministry official leaked information about inquiries into National Rally campaign financing; no one had been formally charged in the reports reviewed.
articles.content:
French authorities are investigating suspected breaches of professional confidentiality and investigative secrecy involving Hugues Moutouh, a former senior Interior Ministry official who is now a regional prefect. Le Monde reported that investigators suspect he may have shared information about inquiries into the financing of the National Rally's 2022 and 2024 election campaigns. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said the allegations would be serious if confirmed. The Paris prosecutor's office told the Associated Press that no one had been formally charged at the time of its report, and Marine Le Pen had not commented. This inquiry is separate from Le Pen's embezzlement conviction: she has appealed that conviction to France's highest court. Neither the leak allegations nor the appeal should be presented as a new finding of guilt.

articles.category: Europe / France / Society / Politics / Public Services
articles.summary: Reuters reported 82,500 participants according to the Interior Ministry and 150,000 according to organisers at Saturday's largely peaceful demonstrations.
articles.content:
Demonstrations across France on 21 November focused on the cost of living and student rights. The Interior Ministry counted 82,500 participants nationwide, including 21,500 in Paris, while organisers estimated 150,000 across the country and 45,000 in the capital. Both figures were lower than the previous Saturday's reported turnout.

About 70,000 security personnel were deployed. Reuters described the marches as largely peaceful but reported sporadic violence, including in Marseille. The protests began in September with students demanding better school buildings, more teachers and university reforms, then broadened into a wider movement involving unions and activists concerned about living costs and police violence.

articles.title: UK and EU agree package on food trade, carbon markets and youth mobility
articles.category: Europe / United Kingdom / European Union / Trade / Migration
articles.summary: The UK government says the package could add up to £17 billion a year to the economy by 2040; its youth scheme is limited to eligible UK and EU citizens aged 18–31.
articles.content:
At the UK–EU Summit in Brussels on 20 November, Prime Minister Andy Burnham and EU leaders concluded negotiations on a package covering food and agricultural trade, carbon-market links, youth experience and closer cooperation on migration and security. The UK government estimates that the package could add up to 0.5% of GDP by 2040, or around £17 billion a year; this is a projection, not guaranteed revenue.

The proposed Youth Experience Scheme would allow UK and EU citizens aged 18 to 31 when they first travel to live, work, study, volunteer or travel in each other's territories for up to three years. The scheme is expected to cover 100,000 participants from each side annually, with first travel expected no later than January 2030. It does not provide access to benefits or allow participants to bring dependants. The carbon-market link is being prepared for operation from 1 January 2028, subject to legislative and technical processes.

articles.title: Russian strike on Zelenskyy's hometown kills two and wounds 60, Ukrainian officials say
articles.category: Europe / Ukraine / War / Security / Civilian Protection
articles.summary: Local officials said a Russian strike on Kryvyi Rih killed a seven-year-old boy and a 20-year-old woman and wounded 60 people, including six children.
articles.content:
A Russian strike hit central Kryvyi Rih, the hometown of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, local officials said on Saturday. Two people were killed and 60 wounded, including six children. The attack caused fires and damaged about 25 apartment buildings, a hospital, schools, businesses and vehicles, according to the regional and city authorities.

The Associated Press also reported that a Russian cargo ship bound for Kaliningrad caught fire in the Gulf of Finland after a drone attack, but responsibility for that incident was not established. Finland said the vessel drifted into its territorial waters and that rescue and environmental precautions were under way. These incidents add to regional security concerns as diplomatic efforts to end the war continue.

articles.title: Trump order requires federal contractors to consult White House before answering Congress
articles.category: United States / Politics / Governance / Congress / Accountability
articles.summary: An executive order directs federal contractors to coordinate with the administration on congressional inquiries and withhold communications the White House considers privileged.
articles.content:
President Donald Trump signed an executive order requiring federal contractors and subcontractors to consult the White House and relevant agencies before responding to certain congressional inquiries. The order says companies must coordinate appropriate responses and withhold communications the administration considers protected by executive privilege. It warns that contracts could be terminated and future federal work suspended for non-compliance.

The White House says the measure protects executive-branch confidentiality. The Associated Press reports that Democrats are preparing oversight investigations after taking control of Congress in January and have identified federal contracts as a major area of scrutiny. Executive privilege has been used by presidents of both parties, but its scope is not unlimited. The order is likely to be tested against Congress's constitutional oversight powers and may lead to legal disputes.

articles.imageNote: RadiantWaves repository portrait; not a photograph of the executive-order signing.
articles.whyItMatters: The order affects the information Congress can obtain from companies receiving public money and raises questions about the boundary between executive confidentiality and legislative oversight.

articles.title: Taiwan warns Canada about economic coercion risks as Carney deepens China trade ties
articles.category: Canada / Politics / Trade / Foreign Policy / Accountability
articles.summary: Taiwan's deputy foreign minister warned that Canada could face political pressure through trade dependence on China, following Mark Carney's meetings with Xi Jinping.
articles.content:
Taiwanese Deputy Foreign Minister Chen Ming-chi told the Associated Press that Canada should be cautious about deepening trade ties with China, citing Taiwan's experience of economic restrictions and the 2018 detention of Canadians Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor. His warning followed Prime Minister Mark Carney's meeting with President Xi Jinping during APEC, where the leaders discussed further tariff reductions and stronger economic cooperation.

Carney argues that Canada needs to diversify trade as it faces pressure from the United States, including a threatened 50% tariff on Canadian vehicles and parts from 1 January. He has said Canada could look to Chinese automakers if negotiations with Washington fail to protect the domestic auto industry. Chen warned that Chinese electric vehicles could threaten Canadian manufacturers and raise connected-vehicle surveillance concerns. These are policy warnings and forecasts, not proof that coercion or surveillance has occurred in Canada.

articles.imageNote: RadiantWaves repository portrait; not a photograph of the APEC meeting.
articles.whyItMatters: Canada's effort to reduce dependence on the US creates opportunities but also requires scrutiny of supply-chain exposure, human rights, industrial policy and national security.
articles.whatHappensNext: Watch for the details of Canada's tariff and trade arrangements with China, any formal Taiwan trade framework and responses from Canadian opposition parties and industry groups.

articles.title: Australia and China agree to establish bilateral dialogue on artificial intelligence
articles.category: Asia / Australia / China / Diplomacy / Technology
articles.summary: Anthony Albanese and Chinese Premier Li Qiang agreed to establish an AI dialogue covering safety, governance and applications after meetings with Xi Jinping during the APEC summit.
articles.content:
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese met Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen and Premier Li Qiang in Beijing during his regional trip. Xi described relations as having undergone a 'comprehensive turnaround' since Albanese took office in 2022 and proposed expanding cooperation in agriculture, energy, the green economy and artificial intelligence. Albanese said the countries would discuss differences directly and that stable relations served both sides.

A joint statement confirmed an AI dialogue on safety, governance and applications. The relationship has improved after China removed several trade barriers on Australian exports, but security disputes remain and negotiations between Australian miners and China's state iron-ore buyer are difficult. The agreement creates a channel for discussion; it does not resolve those wider disputes.
articles.imageNote: No verified portrait of Anthony Albanese or event photograph is currently available in the repository.
articles.whyItMatters: AI governance is becoming part of economic diplomacy. Cooperation may reduce misunderstandings, but it will be judged by practical safeguards and whether both countries can manage security differences.
articles.whatHappensNext: Watch for the first meeting of the AI dialogue and any agreed principles on safety, data, research and commercial applications.
articles.label: AUSTRALIA–CHINA / AI DIALOGUE

articles.category: Asia / Japan / India / Defence / Maritime Security
articles.summary: Japan and India signed a letter of intent allowing Japanese Self-Defence Forces to train at Indian firing ranges, including exercises involving surface-to-ship missiles.
articles.content:
Japan's Ministry of Defense said the defence ministers met in Tokyo on 19 November and welcomed a letter of intent for the use of Indian firing ranges by Japan's Self-Defence Forces. The arrangement would allow Japanese forces, for the first time, to conduct live-fire training in India, including exercises involving surface-to-ship missiles. The ministers agreed to accelerate coordination between their defence authorities.

The two governments also welcomed progress in maritime security cooperation under an arrangement signed in August. The agreement deepens defence ties, but the ministry's statement describes a framework and coordination process; it does not establish that the live-fire exercises have already taken place.

articles.title: Israeli strike kills three Palestinians in Gaza vehicle carrying food, witnesses say
articles.category: Middle East / Gaza / Conflict / Humanitarian Affairs
articles.summary: Gaza's Health Ministry reported three deaths after an Israeli strike hit a truck carrying food; World Central Kitchen said the vehicle was not affiliated with the charity.
articles.content:
Israeli forces struck a truck in Gaza City on 21 November. The Gaza Health Ministry said three people were killed. Witnesses told Reuters that the vehicle carried food and papers bearing the World Central Kitchen logo, but the charity said the truck was not affiliated with it. WCK said the driver had previously worked for the organisation and that the two other occupants were not its employees.

The Israeli military said it was targeting Islamic Jihad militants and that the vehicle had been transporting food to members of the group. Reuters said it could not independently verify the military's account, and Islamic Jihad did not immediately comment. The incident occurred despite the October 2025 US-backed ceasefire, which halted major fighting but has not ended Israeli attacks or resolved the question of Hamas disarmament.

articles.summary: UKMTO reported two tanker incidents near Khasab involving unidentified projectiles; no casualties were reported and the environmental impact was not yet known.
articles.content:
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency reported that a tanker sailing out through the Strait of Hormuz was hit on its stern about 11 nautical miles north of Oman's Khasab. It later reported a second incident involving a tanker struck in its engine room about 17 nautical miles east of Khasab. It was not immediately clear whether the reports involved the same vessel.

UKMTO said no casualties had been reported and the environmental impact was unknown. Iran's navy separately said an oil tanker had caught fire after hitting a naval mine in a restricted area east of the strait, but Reuters could not independently verify the Iranian account or establish whether it referred to either UKMTO incident. No responsible party has been confirmed.

articles.title: Fire at Iraq's Hartha power station kills four and injures 35
articles.category: Middle East / Iraq / Energy / Infrastructure / Public Safety
articles.summary: Four people were killed and 35 injured after a fire at the Hartha power station north of Basra spread to nearby homes; Iraq's prime minister ordered an investigation.
articles.content:
Security officials told Reuters that the fire broke out at about 6 a.m. on 21 November at the Hartha power station north of Basra. It spread to neighbouring homes, and many casualties suffered burns or smoke inhalation. Civil defence teams brought the blaze under control, but operations at the station were halted.

Iraq's Electricity Ministry said the incident involved a gas pipeline supplying the facility. Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered an urgent investigation to establish the cause and responsibility. The station has an installed capacity of 800 megawatts and had been operating at about 400 megawatts before the fire. Officials had not yet published the full extent of the damage or a definitive cause.

articles.whyItMatters: The incident exposes the human and economic consequences of ageing energy infrastructure and the importance of maintenance, safety systems and transparent investigations.
articles.whatHappensNext: Watch for the investigation's findings, repairs to the gas pipeline and any effect on electricity supply in Basra and surrounding areas.
